# STARC Institute (星弧)

> STARC Institute (Chinese name 星弧) is a small nonprofit that helps university students build real products and do real research, as an alternative to pay-to-play research programs and résumé packages (背景提升) that sell the appearance of experience.

Key facts:
- Main program: the One-Person Company (OPC, 一人公司计划) cohort. 12 students, 8 weeks, about 10 hours a week. Each student builds and launches a real product with AI tools, finds real users, and keeps a weekly build log. For undergraduate and master's students, any major. Apply through the application form: https://forms.gle/9kHxzd7byt3BKD2k9
- Graduation is judged by evidence (a live product, real usage data, eight build logs), not by a certificate. Two outcomes: Shipped (at least 10 real external users) and Completed (full participation, fewer users).
- Selective research track (科研合作): rare openings with an active researcher; publication is never promised.
- STARC does not ghost-write, does not guarantee outcomes, and does not sell recommendation letters or authorship.
- Applications are reviewed with school names removed.
- The team is small; names are not listed yet.

## Blog: questions answered
- [Sophomore or junior: should I do research or build a product, and how do I split my time?](https://starc.institute/blog/research-or-product-sophomore-junior.html): As a sophomore or junior, choose between research and building a product by your next step. Aiming for a PhD, make research the main line, because faculty letters and lab experience matter most there. Aiming for a job, a product shows applied skill. Give one about two-thirds of your spare hours and keep the other small, since both reward depth more than splitting time evenly.
- [How do I find my first 10 users on campus who aren't my friends?](https://starc.institute/blog/find-first-users-on-campus.html): To find your first 10 users on campus who aren't your friends, pick one narrow group with the problem (say, students in one lab course or one club), go where that group already gathers, ask about their past experience before showing anything, and set the product up with them on the spot. Expect most people to say no; plan to approach several times as many people as the users you need.
- [Monkey King and Lin Daiyu as a couple: what's the pairing, and is there a game?](https://starc.institute/blog/monkey-king-lin-daiyu-game.html): Yes. There is a free browser game where the Monkey King from Journey to the West and Lin Daiyu from Dream of the Red Chamber are already a couple and you plan their days. It runs on a phone with no download, no sign-up and no purchases. The pairing itself grew out of AI-made fan videos that put two classic characters who never meet into the same modern scenes.
- [Can one person with no coding experience ship a web game with AI in a week?](https://starc.institute/blog/build-web-game-with-ai-week.html): Yes, if the game is small and you check everything the AI produces. We built and launched a web game in five days without writing code by hand. The slow part wasn't code: it was getting images right, which took prompts hundreds of words long. A static host, browser storage and a free counter covered everything a server would have done.
- [Do I need an LLC to sell an app I built as a student?](https://starc.institute/blog/student-product-business-registration.html): No, not to start. Under SBA guidance, if you sell on your own under your legal name, you're automatically a sole proprietor and don't need to register anywhere, and Stripe lets you sell without a separate business entity. What you do need to handle is taxes: the IRS expects you to report the income, and self-employment tax applies once net earnings reach $400. An LLC becomes worth it when real liability risk shows up.
- [Can I use AI coding tools on my senior capstone project?](https://starc.institute/blog/ai-coding-tools-graduation-project.html): Usually yes, but only within the rules your capstone instructor sets, and those vary from course to course. Where AI coding tools are allowed, US university policies converge on three requirements: disclose which tool you used and for what, mark AI-generated code in the work itself, and be able to explain and defend every line you submit.
- [How do I prove my app's user numbers are real?](https://starc.institute/blog/prove-product-user-numbers-real.html): To prove your app's user numbers are real, say exactly what you counted (visitors, sign-ups or active users), over which dates, and from which tool, then keep evidence a stranger could check: an analytics screenshot or shared dashboard, an anonymized user list, and notes from real users. A small number with a clear definition and evidence is more convincing than a big number nobody can verify.
- [How do I post a build log online that's honest and still gets read?](https://starc.institute/blog/honest-build-log-that-gets-read.html): To post a build log online that's honest and still gets read, make each post about one specific thing you learned or decided, show the real number with its context (even if it's small), and say how you used AI. Readers follow a process they can learn from; they don't need big numbers. Never buy followers, invent users or post fake reviews, and say clearly when a post is about your own product.
- [My AI-built website is slow: what can a student actually fix?](https://starc.institute/blog/ai-built-site-slow-to-load.html): If your AI-built website is slow, measure before you change anything. Run it through PageSpeed Insights, check whether it's slow for everyone or only for some visitors, then fix the usual causes in order: oversized images, too much JavaScript, and a server far from your users. For many student sites, those three fixes matter more than switching tools.
- [Mobile app or web app: which should a student build first with AI?](https://starc.institute/blog/mini-program-or-web-app-first.html): For most students building a first product with AI, a web app comes first. It goes live at a link the same day, needs no store review or developer fee, and you can change it in minutes while you learn what users want. Build a native mobile app first only if the core of the idea needs the phone itself, such as the camera, background location or push notifications, and you're ready for store rules and review.
- [Non-CS major applying for product manager jobs: does building your own product help?](https://starc.institute/blog/non-cs-product-manager-own-product.html): Yes. For a non-CS major applying for product manager jobs, a small product you built and launched yourself is one of the clearest proofs that you can do the work, because it shows you found a problem, made trade-offs and got real people to use something. It helps only if it's real: live, used by people who aren't your friends, and something you can explain decision by decision. It won't get you past roles that require a CS degree.
- [Can I talk about a project I built with AI in a grad school interview?](https://starc.institute/blog/ai-project-grad-school-interview.html): Yes, you can talk about a project you built with AI in a grad school interview, as long as you can explain every decision in it yourself. Faculty interviewers aren't checking whether you typed each line. They're checking whether you can define a problem, make trade-offs, test your own work and say honestly what didn't work. Be plain about what AI did and specific about what you decided.
- [Do students from less well-known universities stand a chance in a blind-reviewed program?](https://starc.institute/blog/blind-review-less-known-university.html): Yes, if the review is truly blind and the application asks for things any student can produce. A blind review hides the school name, so what's left to judge is the work you submit. It does not erase every advantage, so the best strategy is to send something a reviewer can open and check, such as a live project and an honest account of how you built it.
- [What's the difference between a student one-person company program and an AI side hustle course?](https://starc.institute/blog/one-person-company-vs-ai-side-hustle.html): A student one-person company program is judged by what you ship: a live product, real users and an honest record of how you built it. An AI side hustle course is judged by what it sells you: lessons, templates and a promise of income, often followed by a pricier next course. The quickest test is to ask who earns money if things go well, and what you will have to show at the end that someone can open and check.
- [Are there nonprofit research mentorship options for undergraduates?](https://starc.institute/blog/nonprofit-research-mentorship-undergraduates.html): Yes, and most of them don't advertise. The biggest are NSF-funded REU summer programs, which pay participants rather than charging them, your own university's undergraduate research office, and joining a professor's lab directly. Small independent nonprofits exist too, but judge any program by its written rules, not by the word "nonprofit".
- [Can I build a real product with AI if I can't code?](https://starc.institute/blog/build-product-with-ai-without-coding.html): Yes. AI coding assistants now let a non-programmer build and launch a small, working web product, as long as the problem is narrow and you're willing to read error messages and test everything yourself. The hard part was never typing code. It's choosing a real problem, finding users, and judging whether what the AI produced actually works.
- [Are paid research internships worth it?](https://starc.institute/blog/are-paid-research-internships-worth-it.html): Sometimes, but far less often than the price suggests. A paid program is worth considering only if you'll do real work on a real question with an active researcher, and they'll tell you plainly what you will and won't get. If a program promises a publication, an admission advantage or a recommendation letter in exchange for a fee, treat that as a warning sign, not a feature.

## Game: 圣黛故事 (Shengdai Story)
- [圣黛故事](https://starc.institute/games/shengdai/): a daily-life romance web game starring the Monkey King and Lin Daiyu (the 圣黛CP fan pairing), synced to the real calendar. Game introduction: https://starc.institute/games/shengdai/intro.html

## Tools for the agent era
Overview: https://starc.institute/demos/
- [Agent Field Guide](https://starc.institute/demos/agent-analytics/): reads a web server access log and shows which AI crawlers and agents (GPTBot, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot, ChatGPT-User and others) visited, what they read, which 404s they hit, and drafts a robots.txt. Logs are processed on the user's device.
- [Tidy](https://starc.institute/demos/data-tidy/): scores a CSV for AI-agent readiness, cleans it (dates, nulls, duplicates, category spellings, units) and exports a data dictionary.
- [Agent Replay](https://starc.institute/demos/agent-replay/): replays a Claude Code .jsonl transcript or OpenAI-style message log as a scrubbable timeline of tool calls, errors and tokens.
- [Ship Log](https://starc.institute/demos/ship-log/): a weekly log of what a founder actually shipped, with streaks and a shareable recap card.
